problem: Standard RL cannot learn directly from images: the visual input space is huge and noisy (Bellman's curse of dimensionality). Prior vision-based RL systems relied on hand-coded, task-specific preprocessing to extract state variables, or, like Iida et al., on drastically downscaled monochrome images that only work in highly controlled environments.
motivation: Purposive vision argues that visual skills should be acquired through task-driven interaction, with no supervisor. Local-appearance features (interest points plus descriptors) are robust and task-independent, and a few highly informative ones are usually enough to tell apart the situations that need different actions. The authors therefore propose adaptive-resolution RL (in the spirit of U-Tree) that discretizes the visual space by the presence or absence of selected local descriptors.
key_idea: Place an incrementally grown feature-based image classifier in front of a standard RL algorithm. Visual classes whose Bellman residuals have high variance (perceptual aliasing) are refined by testing the local descriptor, or spatial composite of descriptors, that most reduces residual variance.
insight: In a deterministic, fully observable task, a non-zero Bellman residual (TD error under the mapped MDP's optimal Q) signals perceptual aliasing. Its variance therefore serves as a self-supervised splitting signal, and CART-style variance reduction ranks candidate features drawn from a possibly infinite feature space. The greedy splitting overfits. Periodically merging classes that are equivalent under optimal-value and optimal-policy criteria, with classes represented as BDDs so arbitrary unions are possible, cuts visual classes from 281 to 59 (close to the 44 physical states) and lowers test error from 8% to 4.5% on the campus task. When individual point features are identical across states (the velocity-gauge images in visual Car-on-the-Hill), task-driven composite features built from pairwise feature distances are required and suffice.
method: Image classifier + embedded RL: a binary decision tree (later BDDs) maps each image to a visual class by testing presence/absence of visual features. Model-based RL (a mapped MDP estimated from relative frequencies of the class-mapped interaction sequence) computes Q'*_k for each classifier C_k.

Aliasing detector: computes stochastic Bellman residuals Δ_t = r_{t+1} + γ max_a' Q'*_k(C_k(s_{t+1}),a') − Q'*_k(C_k(s_t),a_t) over a static database of interactions. A class is flagged as aliased if the variance of Δ_t for some action exceeds threshold τ.

Feature generator/selector: candidate features are the local descriptors (SIFT or color differential invariants) at all interest points of images in the aliased class. The feature minimizing the weighted variance of Δ_t (CART regression splitting rule) is selected, subject to a Student's t-test that the two induced distributions differ significantly. At most a bounded number of classes (largest first) are split per stage.

Compaction via BDDs: each visual class is represented by a Binary Decision Diagram over feature literals. Refinement is B(V)∧f / B(V)∧¬f. Periodically (every 10 steps in experiments), classes equivalent under the conjunction of optimal-value and optimal-policy equivalence (threshold ε) are merged by disjunction, with variable reordering to drop useless features.

Composite spatial features: when primitives are not discriminative enough, highly co-occurring feature pairs are searched for typical inter-feature distances via hierarchical clustering of the distance set. Each cluster yields a composite feature with a Gaussian distance model (μ, σ), detected recursively with likelihood threshold ν and located at the midpoint. Hierarchies of arbitrary height form a binary DAG, and irrelevant composites are filtered by the variance-reduction selector.

setting.backbone: Feature-based decision tree / BDD image classifier over local descriptors (SIFT or color differential invariants) + tabular model-based RL on the mapped MDP (trained from scratch, no neural network)
setting.training_data: Static databases of 10,000 interactions collected with a fully randomized exploration policy for each task. Campus task: 24 images of 1024x768 per (location, heading) for 44 states, of which 18 are used for learning and 6 held out for testing. Maze tasks: COIL-100 montage tapestry (1280x1280) or a 3041x384 subway panorama. Car-on-the-Hill: COIL-100 ground montage plus rendered velocity gauge.
setting.observation: Monocular RGB image patch. Maze: top-down view of the ground under the agent. Campus: forward-facing photo. Car-on-the-Hill: two cameras, one on the ground and one on a velocity gauge. No position or pose given.
setting.action_space: Discrete. Maze: up/right/down/left moves with Gaussian noise (std 2% of maze size) in continuous space. Campus: turn left / turn right / move forward on a graph of 11 locations x 4 headings. Car-on-the-Hill: thrust ±4 N.
setting.simulator: Custom simulated tasks built from image databases (no standard embodied simulator)
setting.privileged: none at test time (the optimal policy with ground-truth state is used only as the evaluation reference / comparison)

numbers_note: No standard benchmarks. The COIL maze and subway maze report only descriptive counts: maze 200 of 2298 features selected, 205 classes, k=84, 35 min; subway 144 of 3739 features, 149 classes, 101 iterations, 159 min. Quality for these is shown only as policy/value-function figures. For Car-on-the-Hill (157 classes, 91 selected features, k=38), missed-goal rates and trial lengths over 10,000 trials per iteration are given only in Figures 13-14, not as numbers. Error-rate curves for the campus task are also in figures.
results: RLVC learns near-optimal direct image-to-action mappings on a noisy continuous visual maze (COIL-100 tapestry and a real subway panorama), with value functions closely matching the GT-position optimum. On the Montefiore campus navigation task with held-out images, BDD-based class merging improves test error from 8% (basic RLVC) to 4.5%, with 59 instead of 281 visual classes and 171 instead of 264 features. On visual Car-on-the-Hill, composite spatial features let RLVC solve a task where point features alone fail. After k>27 its missed-goal rate is lower than a direct-perception 13x13 grid baseline, and trial lengths approach that baseline.
limitations: Assumes a fully observable MDP from a single image; no memory for partially observable settings. Evaluated only in small simulated or image-database tasks with discrete actions, with no real-robot deployment.

Relies on static randomly-collected interaction databases and on thresholds (τ, ε, ν, co-occurrence counts). Compaction adds computational cost, and the equivalence relations lack theoretical justification.
Composite features encode only inter-feature distances (no orientation or scale), and continuous action spaces are not supported.
compares_to: Direct-perception RL with ground-truth discretized state (x,y grid / (p,s) 13x13 grid)
